nameStory: The Pure Green Sweat Bee gets its name from its stunning, almost metallic green coloration that seems to glow in sunlight. Like other sweat bees, it's attracted to the salt in human perspiration and will actually lick sweat from your skin! The scientific name Augochlora pura literally means "pure golden green," which is so musical that some experts think it doesn't even need a common name.
description: The Pure Green Sweat Bee is a small, solitary bee that looks like a tiny emerald flying through the forest. Its entire body shines with an iridescent green color that can appear almost metallic in bright light. Unlike honeybees that live in large colonies, these bees live alone and make their homes in rotting logs. They're about the size of a small honeybee but much more brilliantly colored.

idTips.label: Brilliant Green Color
idTips.description: The entire body gleams with a bright, metallic green that catches light like a jewel - unmistakable when you see it

idTips.label: Small Solitary Bee Size
idTips.description: About the size of a small honeybee, but stockier and more compact in build

idTips.label: Attraction to Sweat
idTips.description: May land on you and gently lick your skin for salt - feels like a tiny, tickling tongue

idTips.label: Rotting Wood Association
idTips.description: Often seen flying around or emerging from decaying logs that feel soft and spongy to the touch

idTips.label: Diverse Foraging
idTips.description: Visits many different types of flowers, from tiny wildflowers to larger blooms, unlike specialist bees

habitat: Look for Pure Green Sweat Bees in deciduous and mixed forests where fallen logs are slowly decomposing on the forest floor. They prefer areas with a mix of sun and shade, where wildflowers bloom near rotting wood. You'll often find them in woodland edges, clearings, and along forest trails where flowering plants grow alongside decaying timber.

seasonality.spring: First generation emerges from overwintering sites in rotting logs, beginning to forage on early spring wildflowers and tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with up to three generations possible - adults most commonly seen visiting flowers and investigating rotting logs for nesting sites.
seasonality.fall: Final generation prepares for winter, with some individuals still active on late-season flowers before seeking shelter in decaying wood.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate deep within rotting logs, completely inactive and hidden from view.

funFact: This bee can produce up to three complete generations in a single year, which is remarkable for a solitary bee - most manage only one generation annually, making the Pure Green Sweat Bee a speed-breeding champion of the bee world!
confusionNotes: Other sweat bees can be green, but none are as brilliantly and purely green as this species - most have bronze, copper, or blue-green tints mixed in. Memory trick: if it looks like someone dipped a bee in liquid emerald paint, it's probably a Pure Green Sweat Bee!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "sweat bee," these insects are completely harmless and rarely sting - they're simply attracted to the minerals in human perspiration and are actually beneficial pollinators that help many native plants reproduce.
compareHints: The Pure Green Sweat Bee is the only Augochlora species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other sweat bees in the region, it's distinguished by its pure, brilliant green color without the bronze, blue, or coppery tints that characterize most other members of the sweat bee family. Its association with rotting wood for nesting also sets it apart from ground-nesting sweat bee relatives.
